citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.
Assume AC. For $1\le p\le\infty$, conditional expectation is a linear map from real $L^p(P)$ to real $L^p(P|_{\mathcal G})$ satisfying $\|E[X\mid\mathcal G]\|_p\le\|X\|_p$.

derivations.claim: For each integer $n\ge1$, let $T_n(u)=\max(-n,\min(u,n))$. The functions $T_n(U)$ and $h(Z)$ are bounded and measurable, so [F1] gives the identity $E[T_n(U)h(Z)\mid\mathcal G]=E[T_n(U)\mid\mathcal G]E[h(Z)\mid\mathcal G]$ of the classes in [F2].

Since $U\in L^1$, $T_n(U)\to U$ in $L^1$; boundedness of $h$ gives $T_n(U)h(Z)\to Uh(Z)$ in $L^1$. By [F3], the conditional expectations on the left converge in $L^1$ to $E[Uh(Z)\mid\mathcal G]$, and $E[T_n(U)\mid\mathcal G]\to E[U\mid\mathcal G]$ in $L^1$. Also $|E[h(Z)\mid\mathcal G]|\le\|h\|_\infty$ almost surely by [F3], so multiplication by this factor preserves that $L^1$ convergence. Taking the $L^1$ limits in step 1.1 proves the stated identity of almost-sure classes.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix a target population with probability law $P$, a real outcome, and a nonempty countable discrete set $\mathcal A$ of treatment versions. A treatment version $a\in\mathcal A$ is a specified intervention protocol, not just a treatment label. The **potential outcome** $Y^a$ is the real random variable giving the outcome for a unit in the target population under version $a$. Write $A$ for the observed treatment assignment or receipt, with values in $\mathcal A$, and $Y$ for the observed outcome. The **observed potential outcome** is the measurable random variable

$$Y^A=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}\mathbf 1_{\{A=a\}}Y^a,$$

where the countable sum has at most one nonzero summand at each sample point. **Consistency** is the assumption $Y=Y^A$ $P$-almost surely. It links the observed outcome to the potential outcome for the received version; it does not assert that treatment assignment is unconfounded.

The **full-data law** is the joint law of the potential-outcome family, $A$, any baseline covariate random element $L$, and $Y$. The **observed-data law** is its marginal law of $(A,L,Y)$. A target population, outcome, intervention protocol, and contrast must be fixed before the associated causal target is specified. If interference between units matters, the version or treatment regime must include the relevant assignment or exposure of other units; the notation $Y^a$ by itself does not assert no interference.

Let $A$ be the observed treatment assignment, $L$ a baseline covariate random element, and $(Y^a)_{a\in\mathcal A}$ the potential-outcome family of [[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]]. **Conditional exchangeability given $L$** means

$$\sigma(Y^a:a\in\mathcal A)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(A)\mid\sigma(L),$$

where conditional independence is the bounded-measurable-function factorization of [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]] under the [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Each fixed $Y^a$ is then conditionally independent of $A$ given $L$ by measurable-map preservation in [[lem-conditional-independence-equivalences-and-preservation]]. This is a full-data assumption; the observed distribution alone does not establish it.

Let $A$ take values in a countable discrete set on a target probability space, and let $L$ be the baseline covariate random element. For a treatment value $a$ of interest, the conditional treatment probability is the almost-sure class

$$e_a=E[\mathbf 1_{\{A=a\}}\mid\sigma(L)],$$

using the conditional-expectation convention of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]] under the [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. **Positivity for $a$ on the target population** means both $P(A=a)>0$ and $e_a>0$ almost surely under the target law of $L$. Positivity for a contrast is required at every treatment value in that contrast.

The almost-sure condition is relative to the target population: values of $L$ with zero target probability impose no condition. Strict positivity does not mean that $e_a$ is bounded away from zero. The marginal condition makes the observed treatment-stratum law $P(\,\cdot\mid A=a)$ available.

In a fixed target population with two specified treatment versions $0$ and $1$ and integrable potential outcomes $Y^0,Y^1$ from [[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]], the **average treatment effect (ATE)** is the target-population mean contrast $E[Y^1-Y^0]$. For a baseline covariate random element $L$, the **conditional average treatment effect (CATE) given $L$** is the conditional-expectation almost-sure class

$$E[Y^1-Y^0\mid\sigma(L)],$$

using the conditional-expectation convention of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]] under the [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Thus a CATE is determined only up to equality almost surely under the target law of $L$; a pointwise value at a null covariate value is not specified by this definition. The ATE is the mean of the individual contrast, not an assertion that both potential outcomes are observed for any unit.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Assume the [[def-axiom-of-choice]] for the conditional-expectation classes. Let $U$ be a real integrable random variable, let $Z$ be a random element, and let $\mathcal G$ be a sub-sigma-algebra. If $U$ and $Z$ are conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$ in the bounded-function sense of [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]], then for every bounded measurable real function $h$ on the state space of $Z$,

$$E[U h(Z)\mid\mathcal G]=E[U\mid\mathcal G]E[h(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

Assume AC. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable random element with standard-Borel target, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be any sub-sigma-algebra. There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. Every section is a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points, and no countable-generation or completeness assumption on $\mathcal G$ is required.

For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

Assume AC. Let $X$ and $Y$ take values in nonempty standard-Borel spaces $(E,\mathcal S)$ and $(T,\mathcal T)$ on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. Let $L$ be a specified regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, everywhere a probability kernel. There is a probability kernel $K:T\to E$ such that $L(\omega,\cdot)=K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ simultaneously outside a single null set. In fact, with the stated everywhere-kernel convention, the construction below gives this equality for every $\omega$. Consequently K is a conditional law of X given Y.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Let $K$ be a specified regular conditional distribution of $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ given $\mathcal G$. For measurable $f:E\to[0,\infty]$, the measurable function $I_f(\omega)=\int f(x)K(\omega,dx)$ satisfies

$$\int_H I_f\,dP=\int_H f(X)\,dP\qquad(H\in\mathcal G).$$

This assertion is choice-free. Under AC, it says $I_f=E[f(X)\mid\mathcal G]$ as nonnegative almost-sure classes. If $f:E\to\mathbb R$ is measurable and $E|f(X)|<\infty$, put $D=\{I_{|f|}<\infty\}$. Then $D\in\mathcal G$, $P(D)=1$, and the signed integral on $D$, extended by zero off $D$, is a real integrable conditional-expectation version of $f(X)$. Its identification with the AC-based conditional-expectation class uses AC only for that class convention.
If $Y,Z$ are conditional-expectation versions of the same real integrable $X$ given $\mathcal G$, then $Y=Z$ almost surely.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

derivations.claim: Fix a treatment value $a$ satisfying the hypotheses, write $e_a=E[\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}\mid\sigma(L)]$, and define $P_a(C)=P(C\cap\{A=a\})/P(A=a)$. For every Borel $B\subseteq\mathcal L$, the defining event-integral identity for $e_a$ gives $P_a(L\in B)=E_P[\mathbf1_{\{L\in B\}}e_a]/P(A=a)$.

Under $P_a$, $Y$ is integrable because $Y=Y^a$ on $\{A=a\}$ by consistency and $E_{P_a}|Y|=E_P[\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}|Y^a|]/P(A=a)\le E_P|Y^a|/P(A=a)$. By [A1, F7, F8], choose a conditional law $K_a(l,dy)$ of $Y$ given $L$ under $P_a$; [F9] makes its zero-filled integral $m_a(L)$ a real integrable version of $E_{P_a}[Y\mid\sigma(L)]$.

Put $v_a=E_P[Y^a\mid\sigma(L)]$. Conditional independence in [F2], applied to the coordinate $Y^a$ and the bounded indicator $\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}$, together with [F6], gives $E_P[\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}Y^a\mid\sigma(L)]=e_a v_a$ almost surely.

The covariate laws $P_{a,L}$ and $P_L$ are equivalent. Indeed, $P_L(B)=0$ makes the numerator in step 1.1 zero. Conversely, if $P_L(B)>0$, positivity gives $P(L\in B,e_a>0)>0$; since $\{e_a>0\}=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{e_a\ge1/n\}$ up to a null set, some $n$ has $P(L\in B,e_a\ge1/n)>0$, so the numerator is positive.

For every $B\in\mathcal B(\mathcal L)$, the defining event integrals of $m_a(L)$ under $P_a$, consistency [F1], step 1.3, and the take-out rule [F11] give $E_{P_a}[\mathbf1_{\{L\in B\}}m_a(L)]=E_{P_a}[\mathbf1_{\{L\in B\}}Y]=E_{P_a}[\mathbf1_{\{L\in B\}}Y^a]=E_{P_a}[\mathbf1_{\{L\in B\}}v_a]$.

By [F5], $v_a\in L^1(P)$. Since $P_a$ is the law conditional on $A=a$ and $P(A=a)>0$,
$$E_{P_a}|v_a|=\frac{E_P[\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}|v_a|]}{P(A=a)}\le\frac{E_P|v_a|}{P(A=a)}<\infty,$$
so $v_a\in L^1(P_a)$. Also $m_a(L)\in L^1(P_a)$ by [F9]. These are $\sigma(L)$-measurable versions under $P_a$ with the same event integrals for $Y$ by step 2.2. Uniqueness [F10] gives $m_a(L)=v_a$ $P_a$-almost surely. Step 2.1 transfers this equality to $P_L$-almost every covariate value, so the integral in the statement is finite and independent of the conditional-law version and its null-set filler.
By [F12], $E_P[v_a]=E_P[Y^a]$. Since $m_a(L)=v_a$ $P$-almost surely on the target covariate law by step 3.1, the change-of-variables identity [F13] yields $\int m_a(l)P_L(dl)=E_P[Y^a]$.

If $L$ is countably discrete, positivity implies $P(A=a,L=l)>0$ for every atom $l$ with $P(L=l)>0$, so the conditional-mean definition in the statement and the version identity [F9] give $m_a(l)=E[Y\mid A=a,L=l]$ there. Splitting the integral in step 4.1 over the countable support proves the displayed sum; its absolute convergence follows from the integrability of $v_a$. For $a=0,1$, linearity of conditional expectation [F12] gives the CATE version $m_1(L)-m_0(L),$ and subtraction of the two mean identities gives the ATE formula. Equal observed-data laws give the same $P_L$ and the same law $Q_a$ of $(L,Y)$ conditional on $A=a$, since $Q_a(D)=P((L,Y)\in D,A=a)/P(A=a)$ for measurable $D\subseteq\mathcal L\times\mathbb R$. Under this common $Q_a$, the conditional means of $Y$ given $L$ have the same defining event integrals, so [F10] makes their measurable versions equal $P_{a,L}$-almost everywhere. Step 2.1 transfers that equality to $P_L$-almost everywhere. Hence [F14] identifies each $E[Y^a]$ and the ATE.

risk_review.notes: Independently reviewed all eight proof steps and all 21 direct dependencies, including the precise AC, integrability, real outcome and standard-Borel kernel hypotheses. Positive propensity gives equivalence of P_L and P_{a,L} without a uniform lower bound; consistency supplies stratum Y integrability; integrable factorization and take-out yield equal event integrals. CE uniqueness first applies under P_a; the equality event is sigma(L)-measurable, hence equivalence transfers it to P. Target integrability follows from equality with E[Y^a|sigma(L)], not from stratum integrability alone. Atom denominators are positive and sums absolutely converge. Both arms are required for ATE/CATE; zero outcomes and constant L are allowed, null covariates and continuous treatments get no pointwise claim. Confirmed nonfatal refuter finding: equal observed laws need only imply the common (L,Y)|A=a law Q_a, never equality of full-data P_a. Repaired step 5.1 using CE event-integral uniqueness under Q_a. Reviewed direct consumers: all use unchanged standardization or nonidentification conclusions, not equality of full-data stratum probabilities. No unmet prerequisite or additional AC use.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for

derivations.claim: The point set has eight equally likely elements, $Y^0$ and $Y^1$ are bounded, and $Y=Y^A$ by construction, so all required integrability and consistency conditions hold by [F1].

Bayes' rule gives $P(L=1\mid A=1)=3/4$ and $P(L=1\mid A=0)=1/4$. Therefore $E[Y\mid A=1]=(1/4)1+(3/4)11=8.5$ and $E[Y\mid A=0]=(3/4)0+(1/4)10=2.5$, whose difference is $6$, not the ATE. The difference comes from the different target-covariate mixtures in the two treatment groups.

derivations.claim: In both laws, when $L=0$ one has $A=0,Y=Y^0=0$, and when $L=1$ one has $A=1,Y=Y^1=1$. Thus the observed law is identical in $Q_1,Q_2$, and consistency [F1] holds in each.
